title: Question 6
stem:
Two coherent sources $X$ and $Y$ of microwaves of frequency $2.5 \times 10^{10} \text{Hz}$ are a distance of $0.18 \text{m}$ apart in a vacuum, as shown in Fig. 6.1.

{{figure:figure_6_1}}

Fig. 6.1 (not to scale)

There is a phase difference of $90^{\circ}$ between the waves emitted at the two sources.

A microwave detector moves along the line PQ, which is parallel to the line joining the two sources and $2.3 \text{m}$ away from it.

Point O is on the line PQ at a position that is equidistant from the two sources.
Point A is the position on line PQ where the intensity of the microwaves is the greatest.

parts.label: (a)(i)
parts.text: Explain why the position of greatest intensity is **not** at point O.
hints: Hint 1: Think about what must be true when the two waves meet at the detector for the brightest spot - how must their peaks and troughs line up?
Hint 2: At O the distances from X and Y are equal, so what does the path contribute? Then add the given 90 degree starting difference to see the total difference at O.
parts.proper_answer: Greatest intensity requires constructive interference with zero phase difference at the detector. At O the path difference is zero, but the sources have a 90 degree phase difference, so the waves arrive at O with 90 degree phase difference and do not fully reinforce.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Recall the rule for brightest intensity**
Imagine sitting beside you - brightest means loudest superposition. That only happens when crest meets crest and trough meets trough. In other words the two waves must arrive in phase, with phase difference $0$, $360^{\circ}$, $720^{\circ}$ etc.

Step 2: **Apply to point O**
At O the distances $XO$ and $YO$ are equal, so travelling gives zero extra phase difference: $$\text{path difference at O} = 0$$ But the question tells you the sources themselves start $90^{\circ}$ out of phase. So the total phase difference on arrival at O is still $90^{\circ}$, not zero. The interference is not fully constructive, so O cannot be the maximum.

parts.label: (a)(ii)
parts.text: On Fig. 6.1, draw a cross (x) to show the position of the point on line PQ where the intensity minimum that is the closest to point O occurs. Label this point B.
hints: Hint 1: The whole pattern is shifted slightly away from O because of the 90 degree start. If the central bright spot A is shifted a little above O, where would you expect the pattern below O to mirror it?
Hint 2: Think about symmetry around the shifted centre - the nearest dark spot on the opposite side of O should be the same distance from O as A is, but on the Q side.
parts.proper_answer: Mark a cross B on line PQ below O, on the opposite side of O from A, such that OB = OA.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Picture the shifted pattern**
Normally with in-phase sources the central maximum would be at O. Here the $90^{\circ}$ starting difference pushes the whole fringe system slightly toward P, so A is just above O. The pattern stays symmetric about that new centre.

Step 2: **Locate the nearest minimum**
Moving away from a maximum you next meet a minimum. Since A is the central maximum just above O, the closest minimum on the other side must lie just below O. For a small shift it is approximately symmetric: $$OB = OA$$ So draw $\times$ labelled B on PQ below O, about as far below O as A is above O.

parts.label: (b)(i)
parts.text: Show that the wavelength of the microwaves is $0.012 \text{m}$.
hints: Hint 1: Microwaves are part of the electromagnetic spectrum in a vacuum - what speed do they all travel at, and what two wave quantities are given or needed here?
Hint 2: Rearrange the link between speed, frequency and wavelength to make wavelength the subject, then check frequency is in Hz and speed is in m s-1 before substituting.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Identify the governing wave equation**
All electromagnetic waves in vacuum travel at $c = 3.00 \times 10^{8} \text{ m s}^{-1}$. Frequency and wavelength are linked by: $$c = f\lambda$$

Step 2: **Substitute and calculate**
Rearrange before putting numbers in: $$\lambda = \frac{c}{f}$$ $$\lambda = \frac{3.00 \times 10^{8}}{2.5 \times 10^{10}} = 0.012\text{ m}$$ This confirms the stated value.

parts.label: (b)(ii)
parts.text: For point A on line PQ, determine the difference in the distances $\Delta x$ travelled by the microwaves from $X$ and the microwaves from $Y$.
hints: Hint 1: At A the waves must end up in phase despite starting 90 degrees apart - what fraction of a full wavelength of extra path for one wave would cancel a 90 degree lag?
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Convert phase to path**
A full cycle $360^{\circ}$ corresponds to one wavelength $\lambda$. To cancel the $90^{\circ}$ starting difference, the extra distance travelled by one wave must introduce $90^{\circ}$ of path difference: $$\Delta x = \frac{90^{\circ}}{360^{\circ}}\lambda = \frac{\lambda}{4}$$ $$\Delta x = \frac{0.012}{4} = 0.0030\text{ m}$$

enrichment.label: (b)(ii)
key_concepts: path difference to compensate initial phase
hints: Hint 1: At A the waves must end up in phase despite starting 90 degrees apart - what fraction of a full wavelength of extra path for one wave would cancel a 90 degree lag?

parts.label: (b)(iii)
parts.text: Use the formula for the double-slit interference of light to calculate the distance between adjacent intensity maxima on line PQ.
hints: Hint 1: This microwave set-up is geometrically the same as a double-slit experiment - identify which distance is the slit separation $a$ and which is the slit-to-screen distance $D$.
Hint 2: Rearrange the fringe spacing relation to make the spacing between maxima the subject, then substitute $\lambda = 0.012$ m with consistent metre units.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Map the microwave geometry to double-slit**
Source separation acts as slit separation $a = 0.18\text{ m}$. Distance to line PQ acts as screen distance $D = 2.3\text{ m}$. Wavelength $\lambda = 0.012\text{ m}$ from (b)(i).

Step 2: **Calculate adjacent maxima separation**
For double-slit interference: $$\lambda = \frac{ax}{D}$$ Rearranged: $$x = \frac{\lambda D}{a}$$ $$x = \frac{0.012 \times 2.3}{0.18} \approx 0.15\text{ m}$$ This is the distance between neighbouring bright spots on PQ.
